text.p: Shells landed near the centre of the Congolese capital Brazzaville on Monday as clashes between a political militia and troops loyal to the president entered their fifth day.
French troops in the city were evacuating their nationals to the French military base. France was sending another 500 troops to reinforce the 450 already in Brazzaville.

Clashes between militia followers of ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso and troops loyal to President Pascal Lissouba began on Thursday after soldiers enforcing a ban on private militias surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house.

It was not clear who fired the shells. In the Bacongo district, which has so far been relatively untouched by fighting because it is the fiefdom of a militia which has so far been neutral, witnesses said a shell had landed killing one person.
France's decision to send more troops to its former colony followed the death of a French soldier in a firefight and reports from French nationals who fled the city of hostility towards them there.
French officials said reinforcements would start arriving on Monday from French bases in other African countries.
The United States on Sunday ordered non-essential U.S. embassy employees and dependents of embassy personnel to leave and advised other Americans to do the same.

Refugees crossing the river to Kinshasa in Laurent Kabila's Congo on Sunday said the fighting appeared to be more widespread than in 1993, when 2,000 people were killed in the capital following disputed parliamentary elections.
They refugees spoke of bodies littering the streets but no reliable death toll was available.
Lissouba's government accused Sassou Nguesso in a statement on state radio on Sunday of trying to stage a coup and urged the population at large to rally round the security forces.
"The government informs national and international opinion that it's a question of a coup attempt by Denis Sassou Nguesso who once again wants to take power by force of arms," it said.
"The government asks the Congolese people to stay vigilant and support the security forces to save our young democracy."
A spokesman for Sassou Nguesso said that they were simply defending themselves and demanded that Lissouba admit to being the aggressor as a condition for peace talks.

"The aggressor has to recognise that he has committed a serious error before we can go to the negotiating table," Ambrose Noumazalay said by telephone. "It is not a coup d'etat... We haven't attacked, we have only responded."

Sassou Nguesso, a former Marxist military leader, was named president in 1979 but voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of democratic reform. He has accused Lissouba of fomenting violence to postpone the July election.
A national mediation committee was set up on Sunday headed by Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in the 1992 presidential election.

Kolelas called on Sunday for an immediate ceasefire and deployment of an intervention force to act as a buffer between the rival forces. His own militia in the Bacongo district was at the heart of fighting in 1993 but has stayed clear this time.

France originally sent about 450 soldiers to Brazzaville as part of a Western standby operation to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa during the final days of the civil war that brought Kabila to power in what was then Zaire.
